overview: This map groups northern European Bronze Age communities under a very broad label. Its outline reaches far beyond Scandinavia into eastern Europe, so it cannot stand for one kingdom or shared way of life. The examples here focus on well-documented Danish and Scandinavian communities; Denmark’s Bronze Age is conventionally dated about 1700 to 500 BCE.

periods.title: Earlier Scandinavian Bronze Age
periods.summary: Oak-coffin burials preserve clothing and exceptional personal objects.

periods.title: Later Bronze Age households
periods.summary: Excavated farms reveal food preparation, craft work and connections beyond the household.

items.text: At Bjerre Site 7 in northwestern Denmark, a ninth-century BCE longhouse was at least fifteen metres long. Fire pits, grains and food crusts show that much cooking happened at its eastern end. Thin-walled serving vessels concentrated farther west, suggesting different tasks in different parts of the house.

Nearly 1,800 pieces of raw amber were recovered at Bjerre. Some lay in storage pots or compact clusters. Researchers suggest the household collected and stored amber for exchange, possibly obtaining metal in return. A farm could therefore be connected to distant places while producing much of its own food.

Bjerre also produced evidence of flint tool making and small-scale metalworking, including crucible and mould fragments. Bronze Age does not mean people stopped using stone. Householders selected materials for particular jobs, and flint remained useful for cutting, scraping and other everyday work.

sections.title: Clothes, hair and a special drink

items.text: A young woman buried at Egtved in 1370 BCE wore a short tunic and a skirt made from cords, with a spiral-decorated bronze belt plate. Her teeth suggest she was about sixteen to eighteen. Preserved clothing lets us see a real outfit rather than imagine everyone in generic animal skins.

Her belongings included a horn comb, a small bark box with a bronze awl, and traces of a hair net. Such objects connect dress with work and grooming. The burial is unusually rich evidence, so it should not be treated as the standard wardrobe of every household.

A bark bucket from the same grave retained residue from a fermented drink, probably beer sweetened with honey. Analysis also identified berry-related evidence, wheat and bog myrtle. Pollen can preserve clues to ingredients, although it does not supply an exact recipe or prove what everyone drank daily.

sections.title: A seat, a family and a sound

items.text: At Guldhøj, a man buried in the later fifteenth century BCE had a folding chair placed at his feet. It was made from ash wood with dark pitch inlaid into carved decoration. The seat had been otter skin, of which only a fragment survives. Portable furniture has a very long history.

Three oak-coffin burials at Borum Eshøj held an older woman, an older man and a younger man. Wood for at least two coffins was felled in 1351 BCE. They may have been related, but the attractive idea of a small family remains an interpretation rather than an established family tree.

Curved bronze trumpets called lurs had a mouthpiece at one end and a decorated plate at the other. Modern players can produce a range of natural notes on surviving examples. We can hear the instruments, but we do not know the actual tunes people played at Bronze Age gatherings.

The Trundholm Sun Chariot, made around 1400 BCE, places a horse and a decorated sun disc on wheels. The museum interprets it as the sun’s journey with a divine horse. It is a striking model of movement and belief, not an ordinary cart shrunk for archaeological convenience.

A ship appears on a ceremonial sword from Rørby, with crew members drawn as short lines. Related ship images were carved into rock in Denmark, Sweden and Norway. The repeated motif links objects and landscapes across the sea without telling us the names of the people aboard.

These ships, spirals and sun images offer a visual language, but the cited examples are not a deciphered alphabet. This card cannot provide an attested sentence spoken or written by their makers. Their pictures survive more clearly than their words.

ending.text: Around 500 BCE, Danish communities increasingly worked iron from local deposits, marking the conventional beginning of the Iron Age. This was a change in technology and society, not the fall of one northern empire. The vast imported outline cannot give every community the same ending.
